sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Marduk** (*marduk*) ​— Creation, Babylon, ‌Storms · Solar ‌calf (Akkadian Marduk) ​— belongs to ​the Mesopotamian tradition, ​where it is ​catalogued under the ​domain "Creation, Babylon, ‌Storms". The name ​means "Solar calf ​(Akkadian Marduk)"[^1].

Marduk began ‌as a local ​storm-god of Babylon ‌and rose, by ​the first millennium ‌BCE, to become ​the **supreme head ​of the Mesopotamian ​pantheon**. His name, ​written 𒀭𒀫𒌓 (*dAMAR.UTU*), ​means 'calf of ‌the sun' — ​a theophoric compound ‌that binds the ​young animal to ‌the solar god ​Šamaš. In the ‌Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, ​Marduk defeats the ‌primordial sea Tiamat, ​splits her body ​to fashion heaven ‌and earth, and receives ‌from the assembled ‌gods the kingship ​of the cosmos. ​This temple treats ‌him as the ​**paradigm of legitimate ​sovereignty**: the deity ‌who turns chaos ​into order by ​decree, combat, and ‌architecture.

His city, ​**Babylon**, was both ‌a political capital ​and a theological ​statement. Its ziggurat ​**Etemenanki** ('Temple of ​the Foundation of ‌Heaven and Earth') ‌and its temple ​complex **Esagila** were ‌understood as the ​axis where Marduk's cosmic ​order touched the ‌ground. Kings from ‌Hammurabi to Nebuchadnezzar ‌II ruled by ‌his mandate, and ​the king's first ‌duty was to ​maintain Marduk's cult. ​Justice, law, and ​the measured world ‌were therefore extensions ​of his domain.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores the ​name as **Marduk** ‌and serves its ​temple at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/marduk/). The restoration ​needs no distinctive ‌letters or diacritics ​its ASCII form ‌would lose, which ​places the name in ‌Tier 2. The ​plain ASCII form ‌*marduk* survives as ‌a modern convenience ​imposed by the ​early domain-name system; ​the restoration, not ​the fallback, is ‌the form the ‌project defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Cuneiform ​as **𒀭𒀫𒌅**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "Solar ‌calf ​(Akkadian ​Marduk)"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*marduk* survives ​only ‌because ​the early ​domain-name ​system ​could not ​carry ‌diacritics; ​it ‌is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ​**Marduk** ‌recovers the ‌full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address bar. ​The ‌restoration ​needs ‌no distinctive ​letters ​or ​diacritics its ​ASCII ‌form ‌would lose, ​which ‌places ​the name ​in ‌Tier ‌2.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ‌**m** ​→ ​**M** — ​Same
‌- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ‌Same
​- **r** ​→ ​**r** ‌— Same
​- ‌**d** ​→ **d** ‌— ​Same
‌- **u** ‌→ ​**u** ​— Same
​- ​**k** ‌→ **k** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/marˈduk/** — ​Akkadian Conventional ​Reading.[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Mar-** — ​Akkadian /mar/ — ‌the first ​syllable of the ​conventional reading, ‌identical to ​the Sumerogram AMAR ‌('calf, young ​animal').
- **-duk** ‌— Akkadian ​/duk/ — ​the second element, ​from the ​sun-god name UTU/Šamaš; ​the whole ‌name means ​'calf of the ‌sun'.

For ​the modern speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation is: ‌'mar-DOOK' — stress ​the second ‌syllable; the final ​vowel is ​short in ‌the everyday transliteration, ‌though some ‌scholars posit an ​original long ​/uː/.

Kindred ‌and historical forms ​of the ​name:

- **Akkadian** ‌— 𒀭𒀫𒌓 ​(dAMAR.UTU), 'calf ​of the sun' ‌— the ​logographic spelling used ‌in Babylonian ​texts
- ​**Sumerogram** — AMAR.UTU ​— AMAR ​= calf, UTU ‌= the ‌sun god ​Šamaš; the name ‌is a ​theophoric compound
- ​**Conventional** — ‌Marduk — ‌the standard Assyriological ‌transliteration adopted ‌into English and ​most modern ‌languages

Marduk ​is Tier 2: ​the canonical ​Unicode restoration is ‌the plain ​Latin form ​Marduk, which preserves ​no diacritic, ‌long-vowel mark, or ​distinctive non-ASCII ​letter. A ​scholarly variant Mardūk ‌with a ​final macron is ‌sometimes used ​to mark ‌a posited long ​vowel, but ‌PuniCodex follows the ‌lexicon's attested ​conventional form. ​The tier classification ​therefore reflects ​the name's ASCII-canonicality, ‌not its ‌religious or ​mythological importance.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Marduk began ​as a local ‌storm-god of Babylon ‌and rose, by ​the first millennium ​BCE, to become ​the **supreme head of ​the Mesopotamian pantheon**. ​His name, written ‌𒀭𒀫𒌓 (*dAMAR.UTU*), means ​'calf of the ​sun' — a ‌theophoric compound that ​binds the young ‌animal to the ​solar god Šamaš. ‌In the Babylonian ​*Enuma Elish*, Marduk defeats ​the primordial sea ​Tiamat, splits her ​body to fashion ​heaven and earth, ‌and receives from ​the assembled gods ‌the kingship of ​the cosmos. This ‌temple treats him ​as the **paradigm ‌of legitimate sovereignty**: the ​deity who turns ‌chaos into order ​by decree, combat, ​and architecture.

His ‌city, **Babylon**, was ‌both a political ‌capital and a ​theological statement. Its ​ziggurat **Etemenanki** ('Temple ‌of the Foundation ​of Heaven and Earth') ​and its temple ‌complex **Esagila** were ​understood as the ​axis where Marduk's ‌cosmic order touched ​the ground. Kings ‌from Hammurabi to ​Nebuchadnezzar II ruled ​by his mandate, ​and the king's ​first duty was to ‌maintain Marduk's cult. ‌Justice, law, and ​the measured world ‌were therefore extensions ​of his domain.[^1]

​### The Winged ‌Sun-Disc

The solar ‌emblem of divine ‌kingship; Marduk's name ‌binds him to ​the sun-god Šamaš, and ‌the winged disc ​proclaims celestial authority.

​### Esagila & ​Etemenanki

The 'House ‌of the Raised ​Head' and the ​ziggurat 'Foundation of ​Heaven and Earth' ‌— the architectural ​center of Marduk's ​cosmic rule.

### The ​Four Winds

Marduk ‌holds the four ​winds as weapons ‌and messengers; in ​the Enuma Elish ‌they are the ​first instruments he ‌fashions for the ‌storm-battle.

### The ​Measured Cosmos

After ​defeating Tiamat, Marduk divides ​her corpse into ​halves, sets up ‌constellations as heavenly ‌regulators, and establishes ​the calendar.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Marduk ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, each ​a ‌compressed ​statement about ‌the ​name:[^1]

‌- ​**Winged sun-disc** ​— ​The ​emblem ​of solar ‌kingship ​and ‌Marduk's ​link to ‌the ​sun-god ‌Šamaš
​- **Spade ‌or ​triangular ​hoe ‌(šaruḫu)** — ‌Marduk's ‌primary ​attribute, the ​tool ‌with ​which ​he shapes ‌land ​and ​clears ‌the primordial ​waters
‌- ​**Mušḫuššu ​dragon** — ​The ​snake-dragon ‌hybrid ‌that serves ​as ‌Marduk's ​sacred animal, ​seen ‌on ‌the ‌Ishtar Gate
‌- ​**Four ‌winds** ​— The ​winds ​Marduk ‌deploys ​as weapons ​and ​messengers ‌in ​the chaos-battle
​- ​**Ziggurat ‌/ ​cosmic mountain** ‌— ​Etemenanki ‌as the ​axis ‌between ‌heaven ​and earth, ​the ​material ​form ‌of Marduk's ‌ordered ​cosmos

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Marduk's mythology is ​the mythology of **cosmic sovereignty**. It ‌is not enough for him ‌to be powerful; he must ​be chosen by the gods, prove ​himself in combat, build the ​world, and then receive the ​legal instrument of kingship. His stories ​are therefore political theology in ‌narrative form: they explain why ​Babylon, and by extension its god, ​stands at the center of ‌the world.[^1]

### Marduk Slays ​Tiamat and Builds the World (Enuma ‌Elish)

In the Babylonian *Enuma ​Elish* ('When on High'), the ‌younger gods disturb the primordial Apsu ​and Tiamat. After Apsu is ​killed, Tiamat raises an army of ​monsters to avenge him. Marduk ​alone accepts the challenge, on ​condition that the gods grant him ‌supreme kingship. He rides into ​battle in a storm-chariot drawn ‌by four fearful creatures, surrounds Tiamat ​with the four winds, and ‌splits her body with his ​bow and mace. From one half ‌he makes the sky; from ​the other, the earth. He ‌fixes the stars, the moon, and ​the calendar, then creates humankind ​from the blood of the ‌slain god Kingu to serve the ‌gods. The poem is both ‌creation myth and charter for Marduk's ​cult in Babylon.[^2]

### Marduk ​Receives His Names (The Fifty ‌Names)

The seventh and final tablet ​of the *Enuma Elish* lists ​Marduk's fifty names, each explained ‌as a function or title he ​has absorbed from older gods. ​Anu, Enlil, and Ea yield ‌aspects of their sovereignty to him; ​his names declare him creator, ‌provider, judge, and shepherd. This ​is not mere praise but **theological ​consolidation**: by naming, the older ​pantheon legally transfers cosmic authority ​to Babylon's patron deity. The list ‌preserves the names of deities ‌who might otherwise have been ​forgotten, making the tablet a kind ‌of annotated divine genealogy.

### ​Marduk and the Gift of Kingship ​(Hammurabi)

The prologue to the ‌*Code of Hammurabi* names Marduk ‌as the god who called Hammurabi ‌'to bring about the welfare ‌of the people' and 'to ​cause justice to prevail in the ‌land.' Kingship is thus a ​delegated office: the king rules ​because Marduk has chosen him, and ​his laws are legitimate because ‌they extend Marduk's own ordering ​power. Nebuchadnezzar II later boasted of ​rebuilding Esagila and Etemenanki, framing ​his reign as an act ‌of cultic service to Marduk.

### ​Marduk's Absence and the Fall ​of Babylon (Erra Epic)

The *Erra ​Epic* tells how Marduk abandons ‌his shrine and the divine ​statue is desecrated, allowing the war-god ‌Erra to devastate Babylon. When ​Marduk returns and his statue ‌is refurbished, order is restored. The ​myth dramatizes a Mesopotamian theological ‌anxiety: even the king of ‌the gods can be absent, and ​the stability of the cosmos ​depends on the proper maintenance ​of his cult. It also reflects ​historical catastrophes such as the ‌sack of Babylon by Sennacherib ‌in 689 BCE and its later ​restoration under Esarhaddon.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Marduk ​absorbed functions ‌from ‌**Enlil** (kingship ​and ​the decree ​of destinies), ​**Ea/Enki** ​(wisdom and ‌water), ​and **Šamaš** ​(justice ‌and solar ​radiance). ‌His rise ​parallels ‌the political ​rise of ​Babylon: ​when Babylon ​was ​small, he ‌was ​a local ‌storm-god; ​when Babylon ‌became ​an imperial ‌capital, he ​became ‌king of ​the ​gods. The ‌Greeks ‌identified him ‌with ​*Zeus Belos* ​(Bel ‌= Baal ​= 'Lord'), ​and ‌Berossus transmitted ​Marduk-Bel ​to the ‌Hellenistic ​world as ‌the ​civic god ​of ​Babylon. In ​Jewish and ‌early ‌Christian exegesis, ​the ‌figure of ​Bel ​and the ‌dragon ‌(Daniel 14) ‌preserves ‌a polemical ​memory of ‌Marduk's ​cult statue ​and ​animal. No ‌later ​deity exactly ​reproduces ​Marduk's combination ‌of ​storm-combat, cosmic ​architecture, and ​urban ‌kingship.[^1]

Kindred ​figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index ​include ‌[[adad|Adad]], [[baal|Baꜥal]], ‌[[enlil|Enlīl]], ​[[keraunos|Keraunós]], [[ninurta|Ninurta]], ​and [[oya|Ọya]], ​each ​linked through ‌thunder ‌/ storm ​sovereignty.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Marduk ​with certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should ​be ​read honestly: ​for ​a ​Mesopotamian ‌name ​of this ‌type ​the ‌material ​record ‌is expected ​to ‌be ​thin, ​and ‌the ‌primary evidence ‌remains ​the ​textual ‌testimony ​gathered in ​the ‌Scholarly ​Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were such ​evidence ‌to ​surface, ​it ​would take ​recognizable ‌forms: ‌votive ​or ‌dedicatory inscriptions ​naming ​𒀭𒀫𒌅, ‌sanctuary ‌or ‌cult ‌remains tied ​to ‌creation ​and ​iconography ​matching its ‌traditional ​attributes ​(winged ​sun-disc ‌and spade ​or ​triangular ​hoe ‌(šaruḫu)). ​Each candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Cuneiform Sources
sections.body: Marduk ​is ‌attested across ‌more ​than ​a ​millennium of ​cuneiform ​documentation ‌under ​the logographic ​writing ‌𒀭𒀫𒌅 ​(*dAMAR.UTU*, ‌'calf of ​the ‌sun') ​and ​syllabic spellings ​such ​as ​*mar-du-uk* ‌and *dmar-duk*. ​The ‌oldest ​certain ‌references appear ​in ‌Old ​Babylonian ‌personal names ​and ​god-lists ‌from ‌the early ‌second ​millennium ​BCE, ‌while the ​vast ​administrative, ‌cultic, ​and monumental ​corpus ‌of ​the ‌first millennium ​identifies ​him ​as ​head of ‌the ‌pantheon. ​The ‌Esagila temple ​archive ​records ‌regular ‌offerings, repairs, ‌and ‌New ​Year ‌(*akītu*) rituals ​that ​enacted ​his ‌cosmic kingship. ​Royal ​inscriptions ​of ‌Nebuchadnezzar II ​and ​Nabonidus ​explicitly ‌invoke Marduk ​as ‌the ​source ‌of legitimate ​rule, ‌making ‌the ​cuneiform record ​as ​much ​political ‌theology as ‌religious ​devotion.

sections.label: Enūma Eliš
sections.body: The ​*Enūma Eliš* ‌('When ‌on High') ​is ​the ​canonical theological ​charter ​of Marduk's ‌supremacy. ​Composed in ​Akkadian, ‌probably in ​the ‌late ​second or ‌early ​first millennium ​BCE, ​the seven-tablet ​poem ​narrates the ‌succession ​of ‌the gods ​from ‌the primordial ​pair ‌Apsu and ​Tiamat ‌through Marduk's ​decisive ​combat. ‌When Tiamat ‌raises ‌an army ​of ​monsters to ‌destroy ​the younger ​gods, ‌Marduk ​accepts battle ​on ‌the condition ​that ‌the divine ​assembly ​grant ​him kingship. ​Riding ‌a storm-chariot ‌and ​armed with ‌bow, ​mace, and ​the ‌four ‌winds, he ‌slays ‌Tiamat, divides ​her ‌corpse to ​form ​heaven and ​earth, ‌fixes ​the constellations ​and ​calendar, and ‌creates ​humankind from ​the ​blood of ‌the ​slain ‌god Kingu. ​The ‌poem culminates ​in ‌Marduk's fifty ‌names, ​each a ​transfer ​of ​older divine ‌offices ‌to Babylon's ​patron.

Foster, Benjamin R. Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature. CDL Press, 2005.

sections.label: Atra-Ḫasīs
sections.body: Although ​the ‌flood hero ‌Atra-ḫasīs ​and ​the ​wise god ​Ea/Enki ​dominate ‌the ​three-tablet Akkadian ​epic ‌named ​after ‌the former, ​Marduk ‌appears ​in ​the background ​as ​the ​established ‌cosmic order ​that ‌the ​deluge ‌temporarily threatens. ​In ‌the ​broader ‌Mesopotamian literary ​economy, ​*Atra-ḫasīs* ‌and ‌*Enūma Eliš* ‌are ​companion ​texts: ‌one explains ​why ​the ‌gods ​created humanity ​as ‌a ​labor ‌force and ​why ​they ​later ​tried to ‌destroy ‌it, ​while ‌the other ​explains ​how ‌Marduk ‌reorganized the ‌cosmos ‌after ​that ‌primordial crisis. ​Some ​late ​traditions ‌and scholarly ​commentaries ​explicitly ​link ‌the flood ​narrative ​to ​Marduk's ‌Babylon, treating ​the ‌survival ​of ‌Atra-ḫasīs as ​proof ‌that ‌Marduk's ​decrees, even ​when ​punitive, ​ultimately ‌preserve the ‌ordered ​world.

sources.citation: Lambert, W. G., and Alan R. Millard. Atra-ḫasīs: The Babylonian Story of the Flood. Eisenbrauns, 1999.
Foster, Benjamin R. Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature. CDL Press, 2005.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Marduk is ​the god ‌of the city ‌as cosmos. ​Where Enlil ​rules the wind ​and Ea ​rules the sweetwater ​deep, Marduk ‌rules the **assembly ​that decides ​what order ‌is**. His power ​is not ‌merely physical; it ​is constitutional. ‌The gods vote ​him kingship, ​name him ​into authority, and ​then witness ​his exercise of ‌it. This ​is Mesopotamian political ‌theory rendered ​as myth: legitimacy ‌comes not ​from strength ‌alone but from ​a recognized ‌procedure, a public ​mandate, and ​the capacity to ‌deliver the ‌goods — ‌in this case, ​a habitable ​world.

To name ‌Marduk is ​to remember that ​creation is ‌not a ​single event but ​an ongoing ‌administrative project. The ​cosmos must ‌be maintained: the ​calendar kept, ​the temple ​repaired, the king ​watchful, the ‌law enforced. The ‌*Enuma Elish* ​does not end ‌with the ​making of ​the world; it ‌ends with ‌the establishment of ‌the cult ‌that sustains it. ​Every ziggurat ‌is a ​promise that chaos ​has been ​defeated once and ‌can be ​defeated again, provided ​the proper ​rites continue. The ‌plain Latin ​spelling of ​his name — ​Marduk, Tier ‌2 — is ​itself a ‌kind of stability: ​no diacritic ‌to argue ​over, no reconstruction ‌to dispute, ‌just the conventional ​form by ​which two and ​a half ​millennia of ‌readers have known ‌the king ​of Babylon.[^1]
